en.text: Climate changes through three external causes: changes in incoming solar radiation, in the composition of the atmosphere, and in the Earth's surface. Nature can act through all three, people only through the last two. Internal causes, the circulation of ocean and atmosphere, move energy around the climate system without changing its total. Today the primary cause is human, mainly burning fossil fuels: the IPCC (2013) says it is extremely likely (at least 95 %) that human influence dominated warming since the mid-twentieth century. People also change the surface: clearing the Amazon forest reduces evaporative cooling and changes albedo, and overgrazing brings desertification.

en.text: The Milankovitch theory, proposed by astronomer Milutin Milankovitch in the 1930s, says three cyclic movements change the solar energy reaching Earth: eccentricity (the orbit changes from more circular to more elongated), obliquity (the axis tilt varies between about 22° and 24.5°) and precession (the axis wobbles). Together they start glacial and interglacial periods; today's forcing is outside that natural range. The sun's own output also varies slightly with sunspots: their number peaks about every 11 years, and at maximum the sun gives about 0.1 % more energy.

en.text: Aerosols are tiny liquid and solid particles from natural and human sources; their effect depends on size, shape, colour, chemistry and height. Natural particles from wildfires, dust storms and volcanoes mostly cool the surface by blocking sunlight. Sulfur-rich eruptions matter most: sulfur gases in the stratosphere form a reflective sulfuric acid haze that can stay for years and cool the surface, especially in the hemisphere of the eruption. Human aerosols from factories, vehicles, aircraft, power plants, furnaces and fireplaces include sulfates and nitrates, which reflect sunlight, and soot, which absorbs it.

en.text: CO₂ strongly absorbs infrared radiation, so the more CO₂ there is, the warmer the surface air. It rises mainly from burning coal, oil and natural gas, and from deforestation, which releases carbon stored in trees. Methane and nitrous oxide are also greenhouse gases; methane causes 21 times as much warming as the same mass of CO₂ over 100 years (book value). Naturally, greenhouse gases keep the Earth about 33 °C warmer than it would be; the problem is the extra gas from people.

en.text: The Earth has been warming since around the start of the twentieth century: global surface air temperature has risen about 1.0 °C since the late 1800s, and each decade since the 1980s has been warmer than the one before. Other indicators agree: glaciers, ice sheets, snow cover and sea ice are shrinking, while sea level, ocean heat and humidity rise and species move poleward and upward. Warming in any one year is small, so it must be judged over decades, not from one weather event.

notes.text: p.44: "NH₃ causes 21 times as much warming" — the gas is CH₄ (methane); 21 is the IPCC 1995 value (later about 28–30). "The other two gases last a short time" is true only for methane (≈12 years); N₂O stays about 110–120 years.

p.42: the text calls the solar-cycle figure "Figure 2.4"; it is Figure 2.5, and two figures are numbered 2.5 (solar cycle and indicators). The Figure 2.5 caption calls the reduced solar activity "the Little Ice Age"; that period (about 1645–1715) is the Maunder Minimum, within the Little Ice Age.
Figure 2:4: the drawing marks 22.2°, the caption says 22.0° (accepted range about 22.1°–24.5°); several spelling errors. The book gives no cycle lengths (≈100,000, 41,000 and 23,000 years).

p.40–41: the promised "evidence for climate change in the past" and the explanation of "how feedback systems work" never appear; p.43 refers to an earlier CO₂ discussion that this unit does not have. The "internal causes" sentence is incomplete.
Two warming figures: 0.80 °C in the past century (p.39) and about 1.0 °C since the late 1800s (p.45). Both are right for different end dates; the lesson states the period with each number.
Added: the 33 °C → −18 °C step (assumes 15 °C mean), the methane CO₂-equivalent item and the average sunspot-cycle calculation.
